title: r/dogs
tagline: Millions of owners who spend on their dogs without much hesitation.
audience: Serious dog owners — training, health, breed-specific questions. They spend freely on anything that improves a dog's life and are deeply sceptical of anything that doesn't.
overview:
The main hub for dog ownership as a practical matter rather than a cute-photo feed. Discussion is about training, health, gear and behaviour, and the tone is informed.

Commercially it's a research room rather than a selling room: what you learn here about what owners actually struggle with is worth more than any post you could make.
discussions:
Training and behaviour problems
Gear recommendations — harnesses, leads, collars, crates
Breed-specific fit and sizing issues
Health and diet questions
Rescue and adoption stories
loves:
Genuine expertise about fit, safety and durability
Products that solve a real behaviour or comfort problem
Honesty about what a product isn't suitable for
dislikes:
Anything that looks like marketing
Aversive training gear, a hard line for this community
Cute-over-function product design
rules:
Self-promotion is not permitted; this is strictly a discussion community
Product recommendations from the seller are removed
Training advice standards are enforced
approach: Don't sell here — read. The sizing complaints and gear frustrations in these threads are a product brief for collars, harnesses and apparel that actually fit odd-shaped dogs.
tags: dog, pet, collar, harness, training, accessories

title: #dogsofinstagram
tagline: One of the biggest tags on the platform, and dog accounts love a prop.
audience: Dog owners running accounts for their pets, plus an enormous audience following them. Pet accounts need props and outfits constantly, which is a business model in itself.
overview:
Vast beyond reckoning, and the key insight is that dog accounts are content creators with a permanent appetite for new props — bandanas, collars, seasonal outfits, birthday hats.

Gifting product to mid-sized dog accounts is one of the most efficient marketing exchanges available: they need content, you need reach, and the audiences overlap perfectly.
discussions:
Daily dog photos and account-run content
Seasonal and holiday dress-up
Birthday and gotcha-day posts
Brand collaborations and gifted-product posts
Breed-specific community tags
loves:
Products that photograph well on a dog
Seasonal items timed to holidays
Genuine engagement with pet accounts rather than cold pitching
dislikes:
Cold DMs asking for free promotion
Items that are uncomfortable or unsafe for the dog
Overposting the same product
rules:
Paid partnerships require disclosure
Gifting arrangements should be transparent
Animal-welfare concerns get called out publicly and fast
approach: Gift bandanas and collars to mid-sized dog accounts rather than paying for ads. They need fresh content, you need photos and reach — it's the cheapest marketing in this entire category.
tags: dog, pet, bandana, collar, accessories, apparel
imageQuery: dog wearing bandana photo cute portrait

title: r/dogswithjobs & pet DIY
tagline: Owners making things for their pets — and buying from those who do it better.
audience: Hands-on pet owners who make beds, treats and toys themselves. They understand what handmade costs and buy from makers when they can't manage it.
overview:
A smaller, practical corner where owners share pet projects — homemade treats, DIY beds, enrichment toys. It's craft and pet ownership overlapping.

The value is credibility: this audience knows the difference between a well-made pet product and a cheap import, and they'll pay accordingly.
discussions:
Homemade treat recipes and safe ingredients
DIY beds, crates and enrichment toys
Safe material questions — what's toxic, what's chewable
Repairing and reinforcing pet gear
Cost comparisons against store-bought
loves:
Safety knowledge about materials and ingredients
Durable construction that survives an actual dog
Honest cost breakdowns
dislikes:
Unsafe materials or ingredients suggested casually
Promotion instead of participation
Products that look good but fall apart
rules:
Self-promotion restricted
Safety advice around ingredients and materials is taken seriously
Vet-adjacent claims should be caveated
approach: Share your recipes and construction methods openly. This audience respects makers who teach, and the ones who don't want to make it themselves become your customers.
tags: pet, dog, treats, diy, toys, handmade, bed

title: #DogTok
tagline: Dogs in outfits is undefeated content, and the products sell themselves.
audience: A colossal audience for dog content of any kind. Product placement is effortless here because the dog wearing your thing is the video, not an ad inside it.
overview:
Pet content is one of the largest categories on the platform, and it's uniquely friendly to small businesses: a dog wearing your bandana while doing something funny is content first and marketing second.

Unboxing and reaction videos work particularly well — the dog's response to a treat or toy is the hook.
discussions:
Dog reactions to treats, toys and outfits
Seasonal costume content
Training and trick videos
Day-in-the-life pet accounts
Unboxing pet subscription boxes
loves:
The dog's genuine reaction as the centrepiece
Seasonal timing — Halloween and Christmas are enormous
Creators who clearly love the animal
dislikes:
Anything that looks stressful or unsafe for the dog
Overt ads with no entertainment value
Stolen pet footage
rules:
Commercial music licensing applies
Animal welfare concerns are reported quickly and taken seriously
Commerce features require eligibility
approach: Film your own dog using your products doing normal dog things. The product placement is invisible because the dog is the story — and seasonal costume content in October will outperform everything else you make all year.
tags: dog, pet, bandana, costume, treats, accessories, apparel
